routes.description: Establish that people sometimes face genuinely available alternatives, exercise control over which alternative occurs, and thereby possess the kind of freedom capable of grounding responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by supporting alternatives and agent control, answering the inference from pervasive causal influence to exhaustive determination, and connecting that freedom to deliberation, normative requirements, and desert-sensitive responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that genuine alternatives and control sometimes exist and can justify responsibility for the action selected.

centralBridges.description: Explain why causal influence, probabilistic pressure, and reason-giving explanation need not eliminate every genuinely available alternative.
Supply a defensible basis for believing in freedom while addressing challenges to intuition, appearances, deliberation, and reason-responsive belief.
Show why responsibility and normative practices require feasible alternatives or desert beyond purely forward-looking behavioral management.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the incompatibilist and possible compatibilist concepts at stake when control, fixed history, and the ability to do otherwise are compared.
Explain how reasons can make free action intelligible even if the final selection is not determined by a further cause.

routes.description: Establish that behavior remains within an integrated chain of biological and environmental causes, leaving no agent-controlled selection among genuinely available alternatives and no desert-based responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting multi-timescale causal explanation to the exclusion of libertarian control, rebutting intuition-based and practical objections, and deriving responsibility practices that do not depend on retribution or earned moral entitlement.

motionBridge.description: Show that antecedent causation excludes genuine alternative control and therefore cannot justify desert-based responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Integrate immediate, neural, physiological, developmental, genetic, cultural, and historical causes into a continuous account of behavior.
Explain why expanding mechanistic evidence and the absence of causally independent action undermine reliance on experienced freedom.
Show how learning, intervention, deliberative inputs, and behavioral change can operate causally without agent-originating freedom.
Connect causal explanation to rejection of retribution and differential desert while preserving forward-looking social responses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish agent control from randomness so that indeterminacy does not itself establish freely authored choice.
Account for gratitude and other responsibility-adjacent practices through evolutionary and mechanistic functions without presupposing free choice.

sections.title: Causal explanation, influence, and genuinely available alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the integrated biological and environmental causal account exhausts the explanation of conduct or merely influences choices while leaving some alternatives available.

sections.title: Intuition, scientific evidence, and the burden of proof
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether experienced freedom and intellectual appearances supply a rational default, or whether mechanistic discoveries and historical error require withholding or revising that belief.

sections.title: Control, deliberation, change, and reason-responsive agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deliberation, advice, belief formation, learning, and reasons can constitute meaningful control or remain fully intelligible as determined causal processes.

sections.title: Responsibility, moral desert, punishment, and humane practice
sections.rationale: This issue connects the metaphysical dispute to the motion's responsibility clause by testing retribution, innocence, entitlement, blame, and forward-looking approaches to harmful behavior.

sections.title: Concepts of freedom, explanatory stopping points, and indeterminacy
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies incompatibilist and compatibilist definitions, whether choice can terminate explanation at an agent's reasons, and why randomness alone may fail to provide agency.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Behavioral choices arise from causal influences extending from immediate cues and physiology through development, genes, culture, and deep history.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted opening-statement sequence remains in Sapolsky's voice and develops the empirical case he announced at the outset.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the con route's multiscale causal foundation and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a broad and concrete causal account across several timescales.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-influence proposition is clear, though the limits of what influence alone establishes remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples strongly support pervasive influence without themselves being presented as a complete proof of determinism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The progression across immediate, developmental, genetic, cultural, and historical causes is internally consistent and cumulative.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move gives numerous concrete biological and developmental examples, with a bounded gap concerning representativeness and exhaustiveness.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly develops the indispensable central bridge requiring an integrated multiscale causal chain.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move builds an affirmative causal case rather than interpreting a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span links immediate cues, physiology, childhood adversity, genes, culture, and deeper history as antecedents of behavior.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Biological and environmental influences form a seamless causal arc that leaves no explanatory gap in which freely controlled alternatives operate.
moves.attributionBasis: Sapolsky explicitly synthesizes his preceding examples and closes his opening statement before the moderator resumes control.

response.rationale: This constructive synthesis advances the con motion route directly and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring a reply.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the route conclusion but compresses the exclusion inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The seamless-arc claim is recoverable, but the step from pervasive influence to no available alternatives lacks a stated qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that no room remains exceeds what the preceding examples of interaction and influence alone establish.

charity.alternative: Pervasive biological and environmental influence may constrain action without fully determining every choice.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must establish causal exhaustiveness, not merely extensive causal contribution.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion follows only if pervasive causal influence is exhaustive, a central bridge asserted rather than defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The multiscale examples support extensive influence, but no representative evidence establishes an exceptionless seamless arc.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The proposition directly asserts the con motion-level exclusion of free alternative control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The synthesis does not squarely address the strongest distinction between influence and exhaustive determination.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky explicitly synthesizes biological and environmental influences into a seamless arc leaving no room for free will.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Free will consists in sometimes having multiple possibilities available and exercising control over which of those possibilities is realized.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Huemer's opening statement, and Huemer explicitly presents his understanding of the disputed thesis and its implications.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the motion-level pro thesis of genuine alternatives and agent control, without an earlier reply obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the central thesis clearly but mainly defines rather than independently supports it.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly limits the thesis to sometimes having alternatives and control over which is realized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an articulation of the thesis rather than an empirical demonstration, its limited existential force is appropriately framed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The definition consistently connects multiple available possibilities with control over the realized outcome.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move provides conceptual clarification but little independent support that the defined condition is actually instantiated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It states the exact motion-level pro requirement of genuine alternatives and control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The passage states Huemer's own conception and does not depend on construing an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says free will means more than one action is available and it is up to the person which occurs.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Deliberation, advice, evaluation, reward, and retributive punishment would not make sense if people never had alternatives available to them.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous part of Huemer's prepared opening and uses his stated hard-determinist framework throughout.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues from familiar deliberative and responsibility practices and has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it offers several connected practical implications, although their common presupposition is contestable.

precisionFindings.rationale: The examples are clear, but the scope of what would cease to make sense under every deterministic account is underqualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that these practices cannot make sense without alternatives omits live forward-looking and compatibilist explanations.

charity.alternative: Deliberation, advice, reward, and punishment can function as causal inputs without presupposing libertarian alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: Retributive desert is more dependent on alternatives than advice, deliberation, or forward-looking incentives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference relies on the disputed premise that practical and normative reasons require categorical alternative possibilities.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The practices are relevant examples, but their existence does not by itself verify the claimed libertarian presupposition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the responsibility bridge by connecting alternatives to retribution and normative practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move groups practices with importantly different dependence on alternative possibilities and omits that qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer cites reward, retributive punishment, deliberation, advice, and evaluation as practices presupposing alternatives.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Arguing for or rationally accepting determinism is self-defeating because argument and rational belief invoke reasons, while reasons to act require that the action be both possible and avoidable.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer labels and develops the self-defeat portion of his opening, distinguishes prior formulations, and then presents his own connected arguments.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents an epistemic self-defeat argument against determinism and has no earlier opposing reply target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a recognizable inference but leaves its pivotal reasons premise insufficiently defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but reasons for belief and reasons for action are treated too interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical self-defeat conclusion depends on a controversial account of reasons that is asserted without qualification.

charity.alternative: Determined agents may still respond to reasons when reasons are among the causes of belief and action.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal determination does not obviously eliminate normative or explanatory reason relations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core inference equivocates between inability to do otherwise, absence of practical reasons, and absence of epistemic reasons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument supplies an explicit chain but offers little support for its crucial claim that determinism eliminates all reasons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central epistemic bridge by challenging the rational assertibility of determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not address the strongest reason-responsive deterministic account before declaring all argument self-defeating.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer argues that reasons require both possibility and avoidability, then applies that premise to arguments for determinism.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: The felt obviousness of freely choosing is not reliable evidence because compelling intuitive explanations have repeatedly yielded to mechanistic accounts.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator assigns Sapolsky the rebuttal, and he explicitly identifies Huemer's reliance on intuition before supplying counterexamples.

components.text: Whether the apparent availability and control described by Huemer provide evidence that such freedom exists.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the evidential force of apparent free choice by comparing confident intuitions with historically displaced explanations, though it does not directly disprove alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive evidential component but does not answer the metaphysical claim itself.

precisionFindings.rationale: The caution about intuition is clear, though the relevant class of intuitions and degree of unreliability remain broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical errors warrant caution, but the analogy does not establish that introspective appearances of agency are probably mistaken.

charity.alternative: Some intellectual appearances may be defeasible yet remain prima facie justified absent specific defeating evidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical intuitive error does not make every appearance evidentially worthless.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The skeptical induction is coherent, with a material bridge from past intuitive errors to this particular appearance.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple historical examples support general caution, but their comparability to experienced agency is incompletely defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro epistemic bridge concerning justification from apparent freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes intuition as compelling but insufficiently distinguishes fallible evidence from wholly unreliable evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky invokes witchcraft and other displaced intuitive explanations to argue for suspicion toward the felt obviousness of choice.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Determinism permits behavioral change because learning and changed conditions mechanistically alter organisms and their subsequent responses.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Sapolsky's designated rebuttal and explicitly addresses an implication he attributes to critics of hard incompatibilism.

components.text: Whether advice, deliberation, and behavioral change make sense only if libertarian alternatives are available.
Whether reason-responsive change is impossible under deterministic causation.

response.rationale: The reply explains how conditioning and changed inputs alter later behavior, directly supplying a causal account of change and indirectly preserving a role for reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the practical-change demand and supplies a clear alternative mechanism.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between choosing to change and being changed through mechanisms is explicit and consistently maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Mechanistic change is well illustrated, though the stronger claim that change never involves agent control remains under-supported.

charity.alternative: Learning can be mechanistically implemented while also constituting meaningful agent-level control.
charity.decisiveQualification: Compatibility with mechanism does not alone establish the absence of control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal explanation consistently shows why determinism need not imply behavioral stasis or insensitivity to inputs.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Conditioning and rapid behavioral updates provide concrete support, with a remaining bridge to universal noncontrol.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable con bridge explaining practical change within causal determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly answers the claim that determinism precludes change but does not fully address compatibilist agent-level control.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky uses conditioning and altered threat responses to show that mechanistic inputs can produce rapid behavioral change.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Examples of biological or environmental influence do not establish complete determination, and cases involving impairment do not eliminate freedom in ordinary, unimpaired decisions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Huemer the rebuttal, and Huemer expressly identifies examples from Sapolsky's opening before challenging their inferential force.

components.text: Whether the cited biological and environmental influences establish complete causal determination of ordinary choices.
Whether impairment cases justify the inference that no ordinary unimpaired decision leaves alternatives.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the inference from influence to exhaustive determination and from impaired cases to ordinary cases as unsupported, stating that the examples do not establish the conclusion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly isolates two decisive inferential gaps and states their defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply clearly distinguishes causal influence from complete determination and impaired from ordinary cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion that the examples do not establish determinism is proportionate to the identified inferential gaps.

charity.alternative: The multiscale examples may be intended cumulatively rather than as isolated impairment cases.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even cumulative influence requires an additional exhaustiveness premise to entail determination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between influence and determination directly defeats an invalid entailment without claiming influence is absent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source-grounded contrast with ordinary unimpaired choice is apt, though the prevalence of impairment examples is not systematically documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central con causal-chain bridge at its inference to exhaustive determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the cumulative causal case while accurately identifying the missing step to exhaustive determination.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer labels the influence-to-determination step and the move from impaired cases to ordinary cases as unwarranted inferences.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Intellectual appearances are indispensable sources of justification, and challenges to free will themselves rely on intuitive and logical appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer announces a response to Sapolsky's discussion of intuition and continues that epistemological reply through the final delivered context row.

components.text: Whether historical errors show that intellectual appearances cannot provide prima facie justification for free will.

response.rationale: The reply argues that reasoning itself depends on intellectual appearances and therefore wholesale rejection of appearances would undermine the skeptical argument's own justificatory basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly targets the skeptical premise and states the self-undermining consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The justificatory claim is clear, though intuition, appearance, and logical seeming are not fully differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some reliance on appearances is plausibly indispensable, but that does not by itself validate the specific appearance of free will.

charity.alternative: The skeptical argument challenges a class of intuitions without rejecting every intellectual appearance or logical seeming.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selective skepticism can remain coherent if a relevant reliability difference is supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The transcendental-style response is coherent, with a bounded gap from indispensable appearances generally to this appearance specifically.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dependence of reasoning on appearances is plausibly illustrated but not enough to establish the reliability of free-will appearances.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con central evidence bridge by challenging its basis for discounting experienced freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply exposes a burden on selective skepticism but sometimes treats it as wholesale rejection of appearances.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer defines intuition as intellectual appearance and argues that all justification, including logical challenge, ultimately relies on appearances.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Practical difficulty imagining life without free-will-based praise and blame does not make retribution or differential moral entitlement justified.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Sapolsky the floor, and the continuous turn states his mechanistic orientation and consequences for punishment.

components.text: Whether practical dependence on praise, blame, punishment, and reward establishes their retributive moral justification.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes difficulty functioning without familiar practices from their moral justification and expressly rejects retribution and unequal entitlement.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the inference from practical necessity to retributive justification.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates practical feasibility from moral justification and focuses its conclusion on retribution and entitlement.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Sapolsky candidly acknowledges practical uncertainty, though the asserted moral conclusion still relies on his contested deterministic premise.

charity.alternative: Huemer's practices argument may concern conceptual presupposition rather than an appeal to social inconvenience.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing that change is difficult does not answer whether deliberation or desert conceptually requires alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between feasibility and justification is valid, but the positive moral conclusion depends on premises supplied elsewhere.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move offers a principled assertion and practical concession but little independent support for rejecting all differential entitlement.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central pro responsibility bridge concerning retributive desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply strongly answers a practical-collapse objection but partly recasts the broader presupposition argument as mere anxiety.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky concedes uncertainty about social functioning while denying that difficulty can justify blame, retribution, or unequal entitlement.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Deterrence and incapacitation alone cannot explain why framing an innocent ex-convict is wrong while imposing the same punishment on the actual offender is permissible.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Huemer answering Sapolsky's punishment claim and develops one continuous framing thought experiment to its stated intuitive conclusion.

components.text: Whether purely forward-looking deterrence and incapacitation can justify punishing offenders without desert.

response.rationale: The framing case directly tests the adequacy of forward-looking punishment by holding deterrent effects constant while varying guilt, thereby exposing an innocence constraint.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly contacts the justificatory basis for nonretributive punishment with a focused counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thought experiment clearly contrasts innocent and guilty subjects under an otherwise similar forward-looking rationale.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The case strongly challenges simple deterrence accounts, but sophisticated forward-looking theories can independently prohibit framing.

charity.alternative: A nonretributive theory can reject framing because of rights, rule consequences, legitimacy, or epistemic safeguards.
charity.decisiveQualification: The example defeats deterrence alone, not every non-desert account of punishment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The controlled comparison effectively shows that deterrent utility alone cannot capture the intuitive difference between guilty and innocent punishment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment is probative conceptual evidence, though its conclusion is narrower than a general defense of retribution.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con central responsibility-revision bridge by testing its replacement rationale for punishment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection targets the simplest forward-looking rationale but omits several strong innocence-protecting alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer contrasts punishing an actual offender with framing an innocent ex-convict when both could generate similar deterrence.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Scientific causal explanations have repeatedly reduced blame and punishment while enabling more humane treatment rather than causing social collapse.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Huemer's explicit defense of retribution and uses a continuous historical series of causal reinterpretations attributed to Sapolsky.

components.text: Whether subtracting responsibility and retribution makes humane social practice incoherent or causes practical collapse.
Whether causal revision can preserve humane treatment without relying on retributive desert.

response.rationale: Historical examples directly answer collapse concerns by showing humane causal reinterpretation, but they do not address the framing case's specific innocent-versus-guilty constraint.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive social-practice component but leaves the later innocence objection unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical claim is clear, with an implicit limitation from particular medical cases to broader responsibility revision.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support humane gains from reduced blame but do not establish that eliminating desert generally will have similar consequences.

charity.alternative: Medicalizing conditions may reduce misplaced blame without eliminating responsibility for ordinary intentional wrongdoing.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy requires showing that the relevant causal discoveries generalize across ordinary agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical induction is coherent, with a material bridge from selected medical revisions to responsibility practices generally.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Epilepsy, schizophrenia, and learning difficulties offer concrete support, though alternative explanations and generalizability remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central con bridge replacing retribution with humane causal responses.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply presents genuine humane precedents but compresses the contested generalization from pathology to ordinary wrongdoing.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky cites epilepsy, schizophrenia, and reading difficulty as cases where causal understanding reduced blame and improved treatment.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: No neural action has been shown independent of hormones, genes, development, and environment, so expanding causal knowledge warrants caution about blame and deserved advantage.
moves.attributionBasis: Sapolsky answers Huemer's skeptical-induction objection, issues the neuron-independence challenge, and carries its ethical implications through the end of his turn.

components.text: Whether appearances of freedom retain sufficient warrant despite expanding mechanistic evidence about neural action.
Whether dependence on multiple antecedents establishes exhaustive determination rather than pervasive influence.

response.rationale: The challenge supplies contrary mechanistic material relevant to appearances, but demanding a neuron independent of all antecedents does not contact Huemer's influence-versus-determination distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the evidential challenge but misses the decisive distinction concerning causal exhaustiveness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The independence challenge is clear, but its scope shifts from neural dependence to blame and deserved social advantage.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Absence of causally independent neurons supports caution, but independence from every cause is not a necessary condition of all agency.

charity.alternative: Libertarian control need not require a neuron wholly independent of hormones, genes, development, and environment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal dependence is compatible with influence that falls short of determining the final selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference risks treating causal dependence as equivalent to exhaustive determination and then extending it to desert.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The listed neural dependencies are concrete and plausible, but the universal negative and ethical extension remain insufficiently verified.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central evidence bridge by opposing experienced freedom with mechanistic dependence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The challenge imposes a stronger independence condition than Huemer's stated alternative-control thesis requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky challenges opponents to identify neural action independent of hormones, food, genes, development, and environmental connectivity.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Without decisive scientific evidence for either determinism or freedom, the rational default is to accept the appearance that one has free will unless compelling contrary evidence emerges.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer explicitly turns to the larger scientific question and states a continuous epistemic argument from possible testing to the default of appearances.

components.text: Whether mechanistic dependence constitutes compelling evidence sufficient to defeat the appearance of free will.
Whether general historical unreliability removes the prima facie warrant of this appearance.

response.rationale: The reply states a defeasible appearance-based default and argues that neither side has decisive scientific evidence, directly answering the proposed evidential defeaters.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it contacts both evidential challenges, though it does not independently establish appearance reliability.

precisionFindings.rationale: The defeasible structure is explicit, but the broad rule that everything is as it appears has an unstable scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The lack of decisive evidence is acknowledged, but a universal appearance-default principle is stronger than the defense requires.

charity.alternative: Mechanistic evidence may be nondeductive yet still sufficiently weighty to defeat an initial appearance of freedom.
charity.decisiveQualification: A rational default depends on the appearance's reliability and the cumulative strength of contrary evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The defeasible-default inference is coherent, with a bounded gap concerning why this appearance deserves its proposed prior weight.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The acknowledged scientific uncertainty supports withholding certainty, but not by itself the positive default in favor of freedom.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con central evidence bridge and advances the pro epistemic case.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes defeasibility but understates the possibility of cumulative, nondecisive mechanistic defeat.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says neither side has decisive scientific evidence and proposes accepting apparent free will until compelling evidence defeats it.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Scientific explanation does not require determinism because scientific theories may be indeterministic and an agent's reasons may explain behavior without determining it.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer takes the floor after the audience question and gives a compact continuous answer citing quantum mechanics and reason-based explanation.

components.text: Whether scientific explanation must be deterministic and therefore exclude reason-based, nondetermining explanations of choice.
Whether causal explanation requires complete independence from all prior conditions.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the assumed equivalence between scientific explanation and determinism as false, citing indeterministic science and reason-giving explanation as countermodels.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly rejects the decisive explanatory premise and states why the inference does not follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes explanation from determination and provides two explicit kinds of nondetermining explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that scientific or reason-based explanation can be nondeterministic is adequately supported by the counterexamples.

charity.alternative: A deterministic opponent may accept indeterministic theories while denying that indeterminacy supplies agent control.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting explanation-determinism equivalence does not itself establish libertarian authorship.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Indeterministic scientific theories directly refute the universal equivalence, and reason explanation supplies a coherent additional model.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Quantum mechanics is a concrete counterexample, though the warrant for nondetermining reasons as action explanations is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the con causal-chain inference that complete explanation must amount to determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately defeats the equivalence while leaving the separate agency question appropriately unresolved.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer cites indeterministic quantum theories and explanations of behavior by reasons as cases of explanation without determination.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: An agent's reasons can explain a free choice even if there is no further explanation of why the agent selected those reasons over competing reasons.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn follows Huemer's earlier answer and develops his characteristic reasons-based account of libertarian choice.

components.text: Whether a freely selected action can remain intelligible without a further determining cause of the final selection.
Whether every explanatory stopping point must instead be traced to antecedent neural conditions.

response.rationale: The reply gives reasons as a partial explanation while candidly allowing that why one reason prevailed may have no further explanation, contacting the demand for intelligibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the explanatory demand but does not explain how the unexplained selection constitutes control.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between explaining action by reasons and lacking a further selection explanation is explicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Huemer's tentative language accurately reflects the limited explanatory proposal and its acknowledged stopping point.

charity.alternative: An unexplained selection among reasons may be random rather than controlled by the agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Reason citation must distinguish authored selection from mere indeterministic occurrence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reasons can explain action intelligibly, but the bridge from an unexplained final selection to agent control remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account is conceptually plausible but largely asserted and does not compare deterministic or randomness-based rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary pro bridge concerning how reasons can explain nondetermined action.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges the unexplained stopping point but does not answer the strongest randomness challenge it creates.

moves.evidenceBasis: Huemer says an action can be explained by the agent's reason while conceding no further explanation for selecting that reason.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: A decision never becomes an unexplained act of agent selection because prior causes remain operative, and quantum indeterminacy does not supply agency.
moves.attributionBasis: The explicit contrast with the preceding view and the deterministic causal argument identify Sapolsky as the responding speaker.

components.text: Whether the final selection can be an agent-controlled stopping point rather than the product of prior causes or randomness.
Whether quantum indeterminacy provides the relevant kind of freely authored agency.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies an unexplained stopping point and distinguishes quantum indeterminacy from agency, contacting both the prior-cause and randomness demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it explicitly addresses the two proposed routes away from determination, though tersely.

precisionFindings.rationale: The prior-cause and quantum claims are recoverable, though the relevant scale and control criterion remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The randomness point is well directed, but the universal assertion that prior causes always decide the issue is under-supported.

charity.alternative: Agent control might be neither deterministic causation nor mere quantum randomness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting randomness does not exclude every nonrandom libertarian account of agent causation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between randomness and control is sound, while the perpetual-prior-cause premise is asserted rather than established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move gestures toward scale arguments about quantum effects but supplies little specific support in the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary con bridge distinguishing indeterminacy from agent control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply correctly denies that indeterminacy alone yields freedom but does not address stronger agent-causal alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: Sapolsky says prior causes never cease operating and argues that microscopic quantum indeterminacy has no capacity to provide agency.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Known biological and environmental causes leave no room for philosophically significant free will, including attempts to preserve it through compatibilism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Sapolsky, whose answer identifies himself with an unusually uncompromising hard-incompatibilist position.

components.text: Whether any philosophically significant conception of freedom survives known biological and environmental causation.
Whether nondetermining explanation preserves a meaningful form of agency.

response.rationale: The reply squarely denies that libertarian or compatibilist freedom survives the causal evidence, but it does not analyze the distinct conditions of those conceptions.
